title: Why are plain Python UDFs slow in PySpark — each row is serialized from JVM to Python and back (Py4J/IPC overhead), and Catalyst cannot optimize through the opaque UDF — and what is the performance hierarchy (built-in functions > Pandas UDFs > plain Python UDFs)?
shortTitle: Why plain Python UDFs are slow in PySpark

s1_definition.profdef: A plain Python UDF in PySpark is a user-defined function that Spark invokes once per row. It is slow for two reasons. First, Spark's engine runs on the JVM, so for every row each value must be serialized from JVM memory, sent over an inter-process boundary to a Python worker, deserialized, processed, and serialized back — enormous per-row overhead. Second, the UDF is an opaque black box to the Catalyst optimizer, which cannot see inside it to push down predicates, prune columns, or apply code generation. The performance hierarchy is built-in Spark SQL functions fastest, then vectorized Pandas UDFs, then plain Python UDFs slowest.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine the National Bank's main ledger is kept by a fast JVM clerk, but you insist every single transaction be mailed to a Python specialist in another building, who opens the envelope, does one calculation, reseals it, and mails it back — one letter per transaction. The postage (serialization) and the round trips dwarf the actual work. A built-in function is the JVM clerk doing it himself. A Pandas UDF mails a whole box of transactions at once instead of one letter each.
s1_definition.oneliner: Plain Python UDFs are slow because every row crosses the JVM-to-Python boundary and the optimizer cannot see inside them — prefer built-ins, then Pandas UDFs.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A plain Python UDF in PySpark is a user-defined function that Spark invokes once per row. It is slow for two reasons. First, Spark's engine runs on the JVM, so for every row each value must be serialized from JVM memory, sent over an inter-process boundary to a Python worker, deserialized, processed, and serialized back — enormous per-row overhead. Second, the UDF is an opaque black box to the Catalyst optimizer, which cannot see inside it to push down predicates, prune columns, or apply code generation. The performance hierarchy is built-in Spark SQL functions fastest, then vectorized Pandas UDFs, then plain Python UDFs slowest.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine the National Bank's main ledger is kept by a fast JVM clerk, but you insist every single transaction be mailed to a Python specialist in another building, who opens the envelope, does one calculation, reseals it, and mails it back — one letter per transaction. The postage (serialization) and the round trips dwarf the actual work. A built-in function is the JVM clerk doing it himself. A Pandas UDF mails a whole box of transactions at once instead of one letter each.

**One line to remember:** Plain Python UDFs are slow because every row crosses the JVM-to-Python boundary and the optimizer cannot see inside them — prefer built-ins, then Pandas UDFs.

sections.s2_technical:
Spark's core executes on the JVM, and DataFrame columns live in efficient JVM/Tungsten binary format. A plain Python UDF cannot run on the JVM, so Spark launches Python worker processes alongside each executor. For every row, the value is serialized (pickled), handed across the process boundary via sockets using the Py4J/IPC mechanism, deserialized in Python, passed to your function, then serialized back. This per-row serialization and context switching is the dominant cost, often making a UDF tens of times slower than an equivalent built-in.

The second cost is optimizer opacity. Catalyst, Spark's query optimizer, understands built-in functions and can reorder, combine, push filters down to the data source, prune unneeded columns, and generate fused JVM bytecode (whole-stage code generation). A Python UDF is a sealed box: Catalyst must materialize its inputs, call it, and cannot optimize across it. For example a filter that could have been pushed to the Parquet reader now runs after the UDF, scanning far more data.

The performance hierarchy follows from this. Built-in functions such as `F.upper`, `F.when`, and `F.col * F.lit(...)` run entirely on the JVM with full optimization and no boundary crossing, so they are fastest. For example replacing a UDF with `df.withColumn("fee", F.col("amount") * F.lit(0.001))` keeps everything on the JVM. Pandas UDFs (vectorized) transfer data in batches using Apache Arrow and operate on whole columns as pandas Series, amortizing the boundary cost over many rows, so they are typically 10 to 100 times faster than plain UDFs. Plain Python UDFs are the last resort for genuinely row-wise Python logic with no built-in or vectorized equivalent.

A senior nuance: a plain UDF is also non-deterministic to the optimizer by default and blocks predicate pushdown, so even beyond raw speed it changes the query plan for the worse. Always try to express logic with built-ins first, reach for a Pandas UDF when you need custom Python, and use a plain UDF only when neither fits.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank computes a small processing fee on millions of transactions. A developer wrote a plain Python UDF to multiply amount by a rate. On the full dataset it was painfully slow because every one of millions of rows crossed the JVM-to-Python boundary. This is exactly the per-row serialization problem.

Problem 2 — The same logic expressed as a built-in column expression runs entirely on the JVM with optimization. This demonstrates the top of the performance hierarchy.

Problem 3 — Some logic genuinely needs Python (a custom rounding rule from a library). A Pandas UDF processes it in Arrow batches, far faster than row-by-row. This demonstrates the middle tier.

What the code will do: a PySpark demo (`UdfPerfDemo`) that computes a fee on transactions three ways — a plain Python UDF, a built-in expression, and a Pandas UDF — and times each, for Rajesh (SAV2001) and Priya (CUR3001) scaled up.

sections.s4d_java:
```python
# File: src/udf_perf_demo.py
# Times plain UDF vs built-in vs Pandas UDF for fee calculation at the bank.
import logging, time
from pyspark.sql import SparkSession, functions as F
from fees.fee_calculators import plain_udf_fee, builtin_fee, pandas_udf_fee

logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO, format="%(asctime)s %(levelname)s %(message)s")
log = logging.getLogger("UdfPerfDemo")

def spark_session() -> SparkSession:
    return (SparkSession.builder.appName("UdfPerfDemo")
            .config("spark.sql.execution.arrow.pyspark.enabled", "true")
            .getOrCreate())

def timed(label, build_df):
    start = time.time()
    count = build_df().count()       # action forces execution
    log.info("%s computed %d rows in %.3fs", label, count, time.time() - start)

def main() -> None:
    spark = spark_session()
    # 2 million synthetic transactions for Rajesh/Priya and others
    base = spark.range(0, 2_000_000).select(
        F.concat(F.lit("TXN-"), F.col("id")).alias("txn_id"),
        F.when(F.col("id") % 2 == 0, F.lit("SAV2001")).otherwise(F.lit("CUR3001"))
            .alias("account_id"),
        (F.col("id") % 100000 + 1000).cast("double").alias("amount"))
    base.cache(); base.count()       # materialize once for fair timing

    timed("PLAIN  Python UDF", lambda: base.withColumn("fee", plain_udf_fee("amount")))
    timed("BUILTIN expression", lambda: base.withColumn("fee", builtin_fee(F.col("amount"))))
    timed("PANDAS UDF        ", lambda: base.withColumn("fee", pandas_udf_fee("amount")))
    spark.stop()

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
```

```python
# File: src/fees/fee_calculators.py
from pyspark.sql import functions as F
from pyspark.sql.types import DoubleType
from pyspark.sql.functions import udf, pandas_udf
import pandas as pd

RATE = 0.001

# SLOWEST: plain Python UDF - one row at a time across JVM<->Python boundary
@udf(returnType=DoubleType())
def plain_udf_fee(amount: float) -> float:
    return float(amount) * RATE

# FASTEST: pure built-in column expression - stays on the JVM, fully optimized
def builtin_fee(amount_col):
    return amount_col * F.lit(RATE)

# MIDDLE: vectorized Pandas UDF - Arrow batches, operates on a whole Series
@pandas_udf(DoubleType())
def pandas_udf_fee(amount: pd.Series) -> pd.Series:
    return amount * RATE
```

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: 2,000,000 synthetic transactions with an `amount` column.

Step 1: The base DataFrame is cached and materialized so each timing measures only the fee computation, not data generation.

Step 2: The plain UDF run serializes each of the 2,000,000 amounts from the JVM to a Python worker, multiplies by the rate, and serializes the result back. The boundary crossings dominate, so it is the slowest.

Step 3: The built-in run multiplies the column by a literal entirely inside the JVM. Catalyst fuses it into generated bytecode with no boundary crossing, so it is the fastest.

Step 4: The Pandas UDF run ships the amounts to Python in Arrow batches, so the function receives a whole pandas Series and multiplies vectorized. The boundary cost is amortized across each batch, so it is far faster than the plain UDF though still slower than the pure built-in.

Final output (illustrative timings; exact numbers vary by machine):

```text
2026-10-30 06:35:02 INFO PLAIN  Python UDF computed 2000000 rows in 9.420s
2026-10-30 06:35:05 INFO BUILTIN expression computed 2000000 rows in 0.310s
2026-10-30 06:35:07 INFO PANDAS UDF         computed 2000000 rows in 1.180s
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```text
  PLAIN UDF path (slow):
    JVM row ─serialize─▶ Python worker ─deserialize─▶ fn(row) ─serialize─▶ JVM
        (repeat per row × 2,000,000)   ← Py4J/IPC overhead dominates

  BUILTIN path (fast):
    JVM column × lit(0.001)  (whole-stage codegen, no boundary)  ─▶ result

  PANDAS UDF path (medium):
    JVM columns ─Arrow batch─▶ Python: pd.Series * 0.001 ─Arrow batch─▶ JVM
        (per batch, not per row)   ← boundary cost amortized
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Plain Python UDFs are slow in PySpark for two independent reasons, and I always name both. The first is the data-movement cost: Spark's engine runs on the JVM and columns live in efficient Tungsten binary format, but a Python UDF cannot run on the JVM, so Spark spins up Python worker processes and, for every single row, serializes the value, ships it across a process boundary over sockets, deserializes it in Python, runs the function, and serializes the result back. That per-row serialization and context switching is the dominant cost on large data. The second reason is optimizer opacity: the UDF is a sealed box to Catalyst, so it cannot push filters down to the file reader, prune columns, or fuse the operation into generated bytecode, which means even the surrounding plan gets worse.

That is why the performance hierarchy goes built-in functions first, then vectorized Pandas UDFs, then plain Python UDFs last. Built-in functions run entirely on the JVM with full optimization and whole-stage code generation and never cross the boundary, so they are fastest by a wide margin. Pandas UDFs use Apache Arrow to transfer data in batches and hand my function a whole pandas Series, so the boundary cost is amortized across many rows and they typically run ten to a hundred times faster than a plain UDF. A plain Python UDF is my last resort, only for genuinely row-wise Python logic that has no built-in or vectorized equivalent.

At the National Bank of India this came up when a developer computed a transaction fee with a plain Python UDF and the job crawled on millions of rows. I rewrote the simple multiply as a built-in column expression, amount times a literal rate, which stayed on the JVM and ran almost instantly. For a different piece of logic that truly needed a Python library, I used a Pandas UDF with Arrow enabled and got most of the speed back while keeping the custom code. The rule I repeat in interviews is: express it with built-ins if you possibly can, reach for a Pandas UDF when you need real Python, and only write a plain UDF when neither of those will do.
